 Toyota recalls 62,000 trucks for engine-failure issue
 A small number of newer Tundra pickups may see their camshafts suddenly snap while driving, warns the automaker
 Author of the article: By Nicholas Maronese Published Nov 16, 2026 1 minute read Join the conversation You can save this article by registering for free here . Or sign-in if you have an account.
 2026 Toyota Tundra TRD Pro Photo by Toyota Article content Toyota is recalling roughly 62,000 newer pickups in the U.S. over the risk that the camshaft in the engines of a small number of those trucks could snap, causing engine failure, possibly while driving. Specifically, the safety campaign covers Toyota Tundras from model years 2022 and 2023; and 2025 and 2026 if equipped with the company’s 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6, the V35A-FTS. The recall does not apply to 2024-model-year Tundras, nor to hybrid versions or Sequoia SUVs equipped with the same engine.
 Article content Advertisement 1 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Transport Canada has yet to make public a Canadian counterpart to this recall, so it’s unclear how many, if any, trucks are affected in Canada. Toyota has also traced the problem to one particular batch of camshafts from one parts supplier – all installed on bank one of these V6s – and so is rather confident in noting that just about 300 trucks out of those 62,000, or about 0.5%, will actually have this defect.

Play Video 2025 Toyota Tundra TRD Pro | Pickup Review | Driving.ca 2025 Toyota Tundra TRD Pro | Pickup Review | Driving.ca Article content On these affected trucks, though, the camshafts may have been manufactured improperly, and so “could snap during driving,” says the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. If this happens, the engine will suddenly fail, and the Tundra will lose all power to the wheels, which can pose a hazard, depending on whether and at what speed the pickup is driving.
 Article content The remedy is simple: Toyota technicians will inspect the camshaft and, if necessary, replace it.
 Article content The Toyota Tundra was previously wrapped up in a similar engine-failure recall, one launched in 2024 and expanded last year , and then again earlier this year, to cover nearly 17,000 examples of the truck in Canada. The defect in that case was tied to the same V35A-FTS, and specifically metal debris in the crankcase damaging their crankshafts.

 Nicholas has been part of the Driving.ca team since 2018, and writes specifically about classic cars – like his first and currently only car, his 1971 Plymouth Valiant Scamp – whenever possible, though he also enjoys exploring vehicular history, automotive design, and car culture. His specific areas of focus include American cars of the 1930s, ’60s, and ’70s. Summary
 Driving.ca News and Features editor; and a Driving.ca contributor since 2018 Professional writer and editor for over 10 years, seeing publication in some of the most widely read outlets in Canada and the U.S. Specialties include classic-car profiles, automotive history, and stories exploring obscure Canadian car culture Education
 Nicholas graduated from York University with a Bachelor’s in Professional Writing, and a minor in Philosophy. He also holds a Canadian Private Pilot’s Licence (PPL); and has been training to be a concours judge. Experience
 Nicholas started out writing news for Sympatico Autos (later renamed Autofocus) before eventually becoming that website’s chief editor. In 2018, he joined Driving.ca, and was not long after made the News and Features Editor. Nicholas has also contributed to the Toronto Star’s Wheels section; to Hagerty’s editorial efforts; and to an assortment of other publications. Nicholas has owned and maintained a 1971 Plymouth Valiant Scamp since 2012; and previously tinkered on a 1929 Ford Model A. He is a regular volunteer with the Cobble Beach Concours d’Elegance in Owen Sound, Ontario; and a frequent participant in Classic Car Adventures’ Maple Mille event in southern Ontario. Major works by the author
 Nicholas loves exploring overlooked corners of Canadian car culture. For Sympatico Autos, he put together a deep-dive look at General Motors’ disastrous introduction of its European Firenza to the Canadian market; drafted an authoritative history of the built-in-Canada MCV CH4 supercar; and arranged the first wind-tunnel test of a 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona “aero warrior” available online. For Driving.ca, he’s profiled Chris Hadfield’s passion for first-generation Ford Thunderbirds ; proven that pre-war cars, excepting the Chrysler Airflow, were more aerodynamic backwards than forwards ; and unearthed the story of the Ferguson Super Sport, a one-off roadster built in Toronto in the 1960s .
